output.name: Thurenna
output.myth: When Aun was a boy he tied his grandmother's hitch on the mooring post, and Tavo the Gale came down the Leeward sea to shake it loose. Tavo blew until the spray stood up like walls. The knot held. He blew harder and the boat spun on its rope, and still the knot held, for the old woman had pulled it tight with her teeth as well as her hands. Tavo laughed, a sound like a sail tearing, and went west along the shingle looking for an easier thing to break. He found the Child's Box-Kite lying in the wrack with its bone frame snapped, and that was easy. Hesk saw the knot from the pole and wound it into the Leeward line, a hand-span from the Plumb-Line, where Aun's stone measures how far the sky has fallen. It is tied yet at the far end of the sky. That is why we tie our boats with a grandmother's hitch. When a thing will not come undone we say it was tied properly. Do not try to loose it. Check your own knots before the wind comes.
output.finding: Find the Plumb-Line, Hanor, and from it look a hand-span to the north-west for Thurenna, the knot that would not loose.
